title_en: Religious practices of the Uda faith
translation:
Religious practices of the Uda faith

The Uda sect is a community of followers established by Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj (1649–1737). A saying current among the people, taken as the sure mark of an Uda devotee, is "Uda is different from all" (Uda sabse juda). The conduct of the Uda faith differs from that of followers of Hinduism in many social customs and religious rites. It opposes scriptures such as the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas on doctrinal grounds. Its followers do not perform Vedic rituals. This shows itself at the occasions of birth, marriage, and death, where Uda devotees are distinct. The rites of birth are performed without the presence of a priest who would otherwise conduct such rituals. After a child's birth, initiation with the sacred neck-thread (kanthi diksha) is given by a devotee at the guru's seat or a partharu shrine, at one and a quarter months of age or even before. At that time a gathering of men and women is present. A hymn of the Parbrahma-vani (the utterances of the Supreme Being) is sung. A tilak of gopi-chandan clay is applied and the mark of a Vaishnav devotee is given. Tying the tulsi-wood neck-thread, refuge in Shri Hari is bestowed. Sweet prasad (sukhadi) is distributed.

At a wedding, the filling of the gotraj (clan-deity vessel), the installation and worship of the family goddess (kuldevi), and the installation of Ganesh are not done. Instead, the guru is ceremonially received and installed. When the guru arrives for this occasion, he is welcomed at the edge of the village with a procession and brought to the wedding pavilion while dhol-mangal (auspicious songs) are sung. When the turmeric paste (pithi) is applied, the couple first bow to the guru in reverence, and instead of kumkum, saffron is sprinkled while the wedding-invitation hymn (kankotri) is sung. A hymn in praise of the glory of Braj is recited. As the applying of turmeric paste begins, a hymn of the Parbrahma-vani is sung. Bawdy wedding songs (fatana) are not sung in the wedding pavilion; instead, hymns composed by saint-poets of the bhakti tradition on the occasion of the marriage of Ram and Krishna are sung. In the wedding procession, instead of a band, cymbals (kansi) and mridang drums accompany the singing of dhol-mangal, while the women sing the hymn of Raghunathji's little horse (ghodli), a hymn describing the wedding procession of Ramchandraji. In the wedding pavilion, the hymn of Sitaji's sohaila (bridal joy-song) is sung. There is no structure representing the traditional wedding canopy (chori); instead, the devotees of the congregation recite and respond to the saint's sohaga hymn (bridal blessing-song). The customs of the antarpat (screen held between bride and groom), the feeding of kansar (sweet wheat dish), and the pressing of the toe (vinchhi dabvani) are kept. The pole-star (Dhruva) is not shown to the couple as in the Hindu rite; instead, at the verse describing the vision of the Supreme Being who granted Dhruva his unshakable position, the bride and groom rise. There is no dowry or bride-price of trousseau-giving. Bawdy songs are not sung in the wedding pavilion; rather, at the time of the marriage rite, the whole assembled congregation listens with single-minded attention to the saint's sohaga hymn sung by the officiant (gor). At this time no other noise of any kind is made, and if any occurs, it is stopped.

When the wedding party (jaan) comes to dine, the women of the party arrive singing the dhol song of Kanaiyaji's aarti. When the bride and groom rise after being married, hymns of devotional feeling are likewise recited.

Death rites — in this respect this sect stands apart even more from the rest of Hindu society. At the final moment of a dying soul, instead of wailing, the hymn of the lodhi-karaj (funeral rite) is recited to them. The body of the deceased is bathed, dressed in new clothes, marked with tilak and given the tulsi neck-mark, seated in a cross-legged posture with the two palms cupped together, and a coconut placed in them. However, keeping a coconut in the hands is not proper; it is proper instead to keep tulsi leaves in the hand. All who come on this occasion offer flowers and bow, saying "Ramkabir." But offering flowers is not necessary — it is enough and proper simply to bow saying "Ramkabir." The men and women present recite devotional bhajans and read scripture (parayan). Women do not sing dirge-like laments (marsiya); but the fact that some women nowadays do sing such songs is entirely improper.

The men perform kirtan with cymbals and mridang drums. For the funeral procession, the body is placed on a bier (sandhasan, a palanquin) decorated with flowers. The men, singing kirtan with cymbals and mridang, arrange the body on the pyre, and the guruji or a devotee of the partharu shrine places tulsi leaves in its mouth. When the fire is lit from the side, the men present recite the kadva hymn (a verse for the occasion). After the hymn is finished, they go to the house of the deceased and perform Hari-kirtan, then take sukhadi prasad and a meal offering before dispersing. Death is called "taking refuge in Hari" (Harisharan). At the house of the deceased, scripture-reading (parayan) and Hari-kirtan are performed nightly for a set period. No rites of sutak (ritual pollution), kaan (mourning period), the twelfth-day or thirteenth-day rites, or shravani are performed.
